newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea's barter deal with Cargill faces failure.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea's barter deal with Cargill faces failure.

text.p: A $4 million barter arrangement between North Korea and U.S. grain giant Cargill Inc was on the brink of falling apart on Wednesday after Pyongyang failed to comply with conditions of the deal, traders said.

Cargill ordered the vessel carrying 20,000 tonnes of its grain to remain in international waters when it learned that North Korea's share of the barter deal, 4,000 tonnes of zinc, had not been delivered to the port, an Asian grain trading source told Reuters.
"The wheat was set to arrive on June 1 or 2 at North Korea's western port of Nampo. But the ship is on the open sea," the source said.
In a deal struck in April, famine-stricken North Korea agreed to have the zinc at the port and ready for shipment before the vessel carrying Cargill's wheat docked, the source said.
The source said Cargill was negotiating with North Korea to try to salvage the deal.
North Korea and Cargill began talking about a wheat deal in January after the U.S. government said it would approve sales of up to 500,000 tonnes of wheat or rice to the communist country.
Cargill wanted to keep the vessel in international waters to maintain control of its cargo and the vessel itself, the source said.
Once a vessel enters a country's territorial waters, international maritime law requires that it follow the instructions of the port authority, a Seoul trader said.
"Without the port authority's approval, no vessel can come in or go out. It is a rule," the trader said.
"Cargill may cancel the barter trade deal with North Korea and sell the grain to other buyers if it cannot confirm the zinc will be coming," a trader at a major grain firm in Seoul said.
The trader said Cargill, a Minneapolis, Minnesota, grain and commodities trading company, could not delay its shipment much longer due to high demurrage costs.
Demurrage is an extra charge paid by cargo charterers for delaying a vessel at the port of loading or discharging beyond the scheduled departure time.
The trader said the current demurrage cost is about $6,000 per day for arrival at South Korean ports. But he was not sure of the cost at North Korean ports.
The trader said the demurrage cost can vary according to an agreement.
The barter arrangement, which involves $4 million on each side, is regarded as a test. If it fails, traders said Cargill would likely be reluctant to undertake future deals.
The Cargill deal is probably the first direct American grain sale to North Korea since the Korean War ended in 1953 with a truce.
